title: Industry layoff watch: Supermassive, Ninja Theory, The Coalition, and a warning from Warhorse
author: Andy Chalk
text:
The plague of games industry layoffs and studio closures that seemed to explode in 2023 has yet to subside. Just about every week there's news of some new restructuring, closure, or cancellation as the videogame industry, particularly in North America, is battered by global economic forces, corporate maneuvering, and private capital.
Here's the latest news related to the crisis that continues to unfold:
SUPERMASSIVE GAMES
(Image credit: Supermassive Games) In August, three months after the release of Directive 8020, Supermassive issued a statement saying that up to 75 of its employees were at risk of layoff . LinkedIn posts from multiple former Supermassive employees (via Insider Gaming ) indicate that those layoffs have now been completed, and that effectively everyone who was at risk of redundancy was let go.
"More than 70 brilliant people are leaving Supermassive: developers, artists, producers, QA, operations and more," Frank Tindle, IT and facilities director at Supermassive who'd been with the studio for 16 years, wrote on LinkedIn . "Any studio would be lucky to have them."
NINJA THEORY
(Image credit: Xbox Games Studios) It came to light in June that Microsoft was planning to either close or sell off Senua studio Ninja Theory , even as the studio unveiled a new game at Summer Game Fest. In July, amidst the big " Xbox Reset ," it announced Ninja Theory had been sold, but then in September it said two attempts to divest the studio had fallen through , and so it was moving toward a closure instead.
That now appears to be happening, as multiple employees on LinkedIn have reported over the past week that they have either been let go, or are at risk of losing their jobs. (Ninja Theory, like Supermassive, is based in the UK, where a legally-mandated consultation period is required ahead of actual layoffs. Technically, employees in the consultancy process are not certain of layoff, but practically speaking—as seen with Supermassive—it's about as close as you can come without actually being shown the door.)
"It's incredibly sad knowing that we won't get to finish what we were working on," gameplay programmer Katrin Mair wrote about the cuts . "So much care, talent and effort went into it, and I really wish we'd had the chance to see what it could have become."
THE COALITION
(Image credit: The Coalition) It speaks to the current state of the game industry that some developers on Gears of War: E-Day are not looking forward to basking in the successful launch of their game, or even the ongoing responsibilities of post-launch support, but are instead worrying about the possibility of being laid off. Multiple sources at the studio told Eurogamer that confidence in The Coalition's stability as the home of Gears of War has given way to trepidation as Microsoft has repeatedly demonstrated that no one is safe.
That feeling crystallized in September when Gears of War: E-Day story director Juan Vaca was laid off as part of Microsoft's latest round of cuts, just weeks before E-Day's release. Others were reportedly cut shortly prior to that. "We honestly expected the layoffs to hit us post-release, but that seems to not matter now," one source told the site. "Now we're just expecting the next wave, or being reorganised under Activision or something later this year."
Those worries are heightened by the potential loss of performance bonuses tied to Metacritic scores, which are reportedly contingent on being employed at the studio when the bonuses are paid, which one source said "should be near the end of October." Some current employees are worried Microsoft could impose cuts to avoid paying those bonuses: While employees who are let go shortly after the game's launch should still be eligible for the payout, one employee said, "It's hard to believe anything [Microsoft leadership] say anymore after discarding staff in this manner."
WARHORSE: A WARNING
(Image credit: Deep Silver) This one isn't about layoffs or closures, but is rather a prediction of continued heartbreak for developers in North America and Western Europe. In an interview with PC Gamer in September, Warhorse Studios co-founder Martin Klima predicted that efforts to reduce the cost of game development (or at least rein them in a bit) could lead studios to move their operations to "countries that are cheaper ... it's maybe Central and Eastern Europe, maybe China, maybe India, maybe East Asia in general."
That's not an entirely new or original sentiment, and as PC Gamer's Joshua Wolens noted at the time, it's potentially good news for devs in those parts of the world, at least until the vagaries of capitalism catches up. But it's far less upbeat for industry workers in North America already facing pressure from rising costs, generative AI, and bottom-line-obsessed shareholders.

title: Steam sale deep cut alert: this ARPG originally developed for Nokia N-Gage is brilliant on Deck
author: Shaun Prescott
text:
Xanadu Next is a Diablo-esque JRPG originally developed by Nihon Falcom for Nokia N-Gage. Those bullet points were enough for me to grab it when Steam's algorithm surfaced it for me last week as part of the ongoing Autumn sale. I wasn't expecting it to be good, but I was definitely curious.
Some background: Xanadu Next is actually a belated spin-off to the PC-88 game Xanadu: Dragon Slayer 2, which was released in 1985 and is sometimes credited as one of the first action RPGs. It took until 2005 for Nihon Falcom to follow it up with Xanadu Next, and when it did it was a Japan only affair.
A PC version did release a few months after the N-Gage version, but again, only in Japan. That PC version reportedly played much, much better than the N-Gage version , as I'm sure you can imagine, but the fact that the game's overarching design was conceived to work across both platforms is what piqued my interest. As did the fact that, when I googled Xanadu Next, I found many people claiming the PC version—which is the version available on Steam—is right up there with the best of Nihon Falcom's games (which is to say, up there with instalments of Ys, Trails and The Legend of Heroes).
Now that I've spent around six hours playing the 2016 English re-release, I can kinda understand why: this isometric slash 'n' grind isn't brilliant, but it has a lot of cosy charm and a fun metroidvania structure. Like Diablo, there's a central village where the knight protagonist can rest, upgrade and do trade, but outside this safe area the world unfurls via (very light) puzzle-solving, rudimentary but satisfying circle 'n' slash combat, and the unlocking of doors with keys bought in town which become gradually more expensive.
Yep, it's a grind. But it's a peaceful, even meditative grind, and the pleasure of pressing further and further outwards into the labyrinthine and reassuringly blocky world is ample incentive to do so. Discovering new ways the world is interconnected is also a pleasure, and while Dark Souls hardly invented game worlds that cleverly overlap and intersect, I have had a few moments with Xanadu Next that gave me the same thrill of recognition. It's also richly atmospheric in a way that blends cheerful JRPG first village trappings with something mistier and more melancholy.
Xanadu Next is currently 70% off for the Steam Autumn sale . It has a few quirks. This being a rare PC-only JRPG, it doesn't have thorough controller support. There is a decent community controller profile but you'll still probably need to use the mouse at times to equip items. I'd also definitely recommend loading the separate config executable and setting up graphics before heading into the game: it won't automatically adjust to your display. The Steam page says it's unsupported by Steam Deck but ignore it: boot the config first, use a community controller profile, and you'll be good to go.
It has made me want to go back to some other Nihon Falcom games, of which I've only played a couple of Ys instalments. Turns out heaps of them are on sale at the moment.

title: Despite the tragic death of its lead writer, one of the scariest games I have ever played will finally come out later this month
author: Ted Litchfield
text:
I cover a lot of demos for PC Gamer, and some of them really stick with me. Divine Frequency has been a real lost Lenore among those memorable games : It was a rare shooter that managed to scare the living daylights out of me, while also being an amazingly satisfying action experience. I've been up on the widow's walk every night, watching for any sign of its ship returning from the long voyage.
Only, I wasn't watching closely enough. On September 25, developer Abraxaes released a new trailer revealing an early access launch date of October 27 for the surreal and horrific FPS-RPG. Before that announcement, back in March, they outlined some of the herculean challenges Divine Frequency has faced⁠—most notably the surprise death of lead writer Pablo "Artistical" Lamprea. Here are Abraxaes' own words on their friend and collaborator:
Abraxaes Abraxaes Abraxaes Abraxaes Abraxaes Abraxaes Abraxaes Abraxaes Abraxaes Abraxaes Divine Frequency's demo had some truly amazing cosmic horror writing: SCP-style, banal categorization of the unknown contrasting with flowery, expansive, yet somehow not indulgent prose to capture the majestic enigma of it all. title: Exclusive – Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy will let you be a crooked cop, pinning crimes on the innocent, or follow in good boy Gregor Eisenhorn's footsteps
author: Fraser Brown
text:
I have technically solved a lot of crimes from the comfort of my gaming chair, but it's surprisingly rare for games to actually engage with the mechanics of a criminal investigation. You'll chat to folk, maybe use your 'detective vision', and then the culprit is found. Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy asks more from you.
As an agent of the Inquisition, solving crimes and putting away heretics is your business. You don't complete quests, you solve cases, log evidence, make accusations, torture and snoop—all in a universe where your word is law.
Owlcat's given us a quick breakdown of Dark Heresy's detective systems in the video above, but like my favourite inquisitor, Gregor Eisenhorn , I wanted to dig a little deeper and put some questions to Veronika Larionova, Owlcat's senior narrative designer.
Is the detective system exclusively based on things that we've seen in the books and other games, or are there brand new elements that Owlcat created from scratch?
(Image credit: Owlcat Games) What tools do inquisitors have at their disposal when it comes to their detective work?
(Image credit: Owlcat Games) How do NPC companions factor into the detective system?
(Image credit: Owlcat Games) Can you conclude an investigation whenever you want, based on thin evidence?
(Image credit: Owlcat Games) Is it possible to conclude an investigation successfully just through luck—like picking a culprit at random? And will the outcome be different if you got the right person but failed to collect all the evidence?
(Image credit: Owlcat Games) What sort of repercussions are there for getting it wrong?
(Image credit: Owlcat Games) Can the player benefit from purposefully pinning something on the wrong group or person?
(Image credit: Owlcat Games) Can we essentially play as Eisenhorn—not the character himself, of course, but exclusively making the kinds of choices that Eisenhorn would make?

title: Deadlock isn't a MOBA or a third-person shooter anymore—City Never Sleeps has turned it into a horror game
author: Elie Gould
text:
Ignore the section tag for this article, because while Deadlock may technically have the DNA of a MOBA or a third-person shooter, it is actually a horror game, and a bloody scary one at that.
How did I come to this hypothesis, you ask? Well, a few reasons come to mind, including one huge one that loves pizza. You see, I predominantly play Rem, and one of Rem's perks is that he can run around the maze of tunnels beneath the map, farming souls and just generally getting up to no good. Until recently I was largely left alone in said tunnels; I hardly ever play against a Calico and Mo and Krill rarely use them.
(Image credit: Valve) And then came Deadlock's latest major update City Never Sleeps , which brought six new heroes, the first of which being the Rat King . Ironically I actually voted for the Rat King, and that decision haunts me.
Picture this. I'm skedaddling around the tunnels minding my own business when, in the corner of my eye I see something staring at me from the end of one of the adjacent tunnels. It's the Rat King, he's seen me, and he's running my way.
I throw everything I have at the rat but that still isn't enough to defeat him. I decide my only option is to turn tail and run, the only problem with that is that when you're locked in combat the map closes down the exits and entrances to the tunnels, something I forgot until I ran head first into a grated exit. Needless to say I died in that cold dark tunnel, and there wasn't much I could've done about it.
(Image credit: Valve) I have been jumpscared by that bloody giant rat more times than I care to admit. Each time I enter the tunnels now my blood runs cold, marred by memories of him hunting me down and throwing Miguel, Jacques, or Abbie with an I at me.
But the horror isn't restricted to the tunnels. Just the other night I was walking through one of the new districts, Chinatown, and accidentally crossed paths with the enemy Abrams. At first I thought that he might not have seen me. I was wrong. I looked back just once to see him right behind me, before I knew it I'd been shoved into the wall and the enemy Seven appeared out of thin air to solo ult me for some ungodly reason.
Perhaps I'm too horror-coded for my own good, and thanks to this I managed to find myself in terrifying scenarios no matter what game I play. But I'm also of the mindset that any online multiplayer game is inherently scary simply because of the fact that people are unpredictable and are almost always out for blood.

title: Warhammer Survivors is more than just a Vampire Survivors spin-off
author: Fraser Brown
text:
I thought Warhammer Survivors sounded like a neat spin-off—Vampire Survivors in a Warhammer skin, created by Boltgun developer Auroch Digital. Having spent 10 hours with its demo, however, I'm increasingly convinced that it deserves to be catagorised as a sequel.
A lot of care has clearly gone into the hero design, maps and all the horrible beasties trying to eviscerate you, and rather than simply replicate Vampire Survivors, Auroch Digital has included a bunch of novelties and new ideas, like followers and more overt boss battles.
Playing it on my Steam Deck has already had a terrible impact on my sleep routine, just like its predecessor. And with its launch just around the corner on November 10, I think I'm just going to have to accept that I'm going to be very tired for the rest of the year.
Everything you dig about Vampire Survivors is here too
Weapon evolutions, enemies that drop chests with multiple items, arcana, bosses, challenges, upgrades—if it's in Vampire Survivors, it's probably in Warhammer Survivors, albeit with some Warhammer-themed twists. Instead of experience gems, for instance, you get experience skulls (because of course you do). And instead of Red Death, you get Extremis bosses, massive seemingly invincible bastards—until you figure out the trick to destroying them.
Nuln oil is deadly
I have used buckets of Nuln oil in my Warhammer painting endeavours—and yes, I've spilled a lot of it. On my jeans, on my carpet, one time on my dog. But it's never hurt anyone. In Warhammer Survivors, it's been weaponised, damaging and slowing ememies, as well as making them more flammable. You'll also be able to get your hands on explosive dice, which roll across the battlefield before going kaboom! I'm sure there are rules against this.
Each map has a strong theme
The first WH40k map sees you running around a battlefield that's being swallowed up by tyranids. It's aggressively pink and full of horrible pustules and grotesque alien topography. In Age of Sigmar, meanwhile, it's skaven time! Nasty little rodents, glowing warpstones, you know the deal. There's even a map that's just your tabletop, full of paints and measuring tape, where all the game's monstrosities gather together to take you out.
You're not alone
While Warhammer Survivors is a singleplayer romp, that doesn't mean you're all alone. Unlockable characters can be rescued once you defeat the enemies harassing them, after which they'll join you in battle. In subsequent fights, they'll rejoin you when you select one of their associated weapons when you level up. At least one character gets buffs from having more followers, and upgrading his lasgun also lets him run around with his fellow Astra Militarum grunts.
It's tough!
I've poured hundreds of hours into Vampire Survivors, and Warhammer Survivors might be a bit trickier. Battles escalate a lot faster, and it took me longer to figure out good weapon combos that worked to thin the herd. I was a lot more desperate for healing than I'm used to with its predecessor. I think I'd prefer the early game to be slightly less intense, though the issue might be that the demo features fewer weapons and characters, which could be making it feel a touch more challenging than it actually is.
Enemy factions have unique traits
Enemy factions benefit from unique traits that may give you a bit of a hard time. Tyranids, for instance, can be empowered by more intelligent members of their species, which use their synapse power to enrage lesser critters within their radius. So you'll want to take these psychic beasties down quickly. Orks, meanwhile, can get all riled up, kicking off a WAAAGH, where they spawn in greater numbers and become faster and stronger.
WH40k and AoS are completely separate
When you play Warhammer Survivors, you select a universe first. Characters, upgrades and unlocks are specific to each universe, though you will find some passive abilities repeated in both. It feels like two spin-offs collected in a single game.
It already works perfectly on Steam Deck
Vampire Survivors is the game that really justified my purchase of a Steam Deck, and while developer Auroch Digital still says it's working on compatibility, it already feels great on my Deck. It's where I've spent most of my time playing it and I've got no complaints.
It's almost here, thank the Emperor
Cancel all of your plans in November, because Warhammer Survivors is launching on the 10th. And I've got high hopes for it. Yes, it's a spin-off, but it also feels like a proper Vampire Survivors sequel and potentially my favourite bullet heaven since the OG.

title: Gundam Rogue Orbit gave me a sick whip sword, but held back the one thing I want most in a mech game
author: Wes Fenlon
text:
I didn't know I could have an entitled opinion about giant anime robots until I played a preview of Gundam Rogue Orbit, but it turns out I can. I'm mad because they gave me a Gundam with a whip sword straight out of Bloodborne (if Gundam hadn't actually gotten there first in the mid-'90s).
To be clear, I'm not mad at the whip sword itself. I'm ecstatic about the whip sword. It's exactly the kind of esoteric weapon that suggests Rogue Orbit has a real shot at being the kind of action game that I want out of Gundam—one with a bit more melee crunch and nuance than they tend to offer. But I can't help but look this gift sword in the mouth, because months after revealing the game, the Gundam team are still holding back hands-on with the bit I want to see most: a damn customization screen.
Why couldn't I look through a short list of weapons whitelisted for the demo build and have a chance to think: "Whip sword? Yes, I'll be having some of that." The fact that you can customize your mech in Rogue Orbit isn't secret: there's a screenshot of the menu on the freaking Steam page! Here's what it looks like:
Bandai Namco Bandai Namco Bandai Namco That looks cool. I would've loved to spend at least a few seconds pondering stats like "close-range power" and "output" before deciding a 60-foot-tall robot using a whip to channel its inner Belmont while fighting aliens is far too dope to resist, numbies be damned.
Demos always have to strike a balance between showing too much and not enough, risking a confusing amount of up-front complexity or a slice so thin it misses some of the fatty goodness that adds flavor. I played about 30 minutes of Rogue Orbit, which was all action, accompanied by plenty of anime-tinged voiceover about the aliens(?) called "The Apocalypse" that made me think I will probably not pay much attention to anything that happens in this story.
On the edginess scale, though, Rogue Orbit's got nothing on the likes of "XXXG-01D2 Gundam Deathscythe Hell" from Gundam Wing: Endless Waltz—you can practically feel the impending turn of the millennium oozing from every letter in that cursed name. Rogue Orbit may not be the politically tinged deliberation on war I love from the best Gundam shows, but that's okay—it's doing something different, and the combo-heavy action immediately made me feel like the game was on to something.
Rogue Orbit skews a bit more action RPG than Devil May Cry—the combos are just a few repeated button presses, and much of your damage comes from throwing in active skills which each have their own cooldowns. Holding a trigger and tapping Square on a PlayStation pad made my Gundam swirl the whip sword around in a 360 degree frenzy, catching anyone nearby in a flurry of quick hits.
Another weapon, the Sword Lance, almost felt Monster Hunter-inspired, building up a unique meter every time I performed a heavy lunging attack mid-dodge. That meter could then be spent to spawn a "Beam Phalanx" of laser-spewing orbs.
Damage numbers, on by default, increase the sense that in the full game I'll be monitoring skill cooldowns a la Granblue Fantasy: Relink as much as I am focusing on attack timing or perfect dodges.
This is, nevertheless, the closest any Gundam game I've ever played has felt like FromSoftware's sublime Armored Core 6. A gentler, "have fun pressing buttons and watch shiny particles go everywhere" cousin, to be sure, but a cousin nonetheless.
It's sort of a cute full-circle moment: In the pre-Dark Souls days, FromSoftware developed several Gundam games for Bandai Namco around the same time it was putting out Armored Core: For Answer and Armored Core 5. The learner has become the master, and so on. If the current Gundam dev team looked at AC6 with envy and decided to replicate it for a slightly less hardcore audience, I think that was a wise move, and I also think, at least based on my early impressions, that they've pulled it off.
But it still feels like I haven't seen the most important bit. So much of the joy of Armored Core—of any proper mech game, really—is assembling a build before tackling a mission, trying to find that balance of speed and durability, raw damage and ammo capacity, range and up-close stopping power that fits the coming threat.
(Image credit: Bandai Namco) Demo practicality be damned—until I'm putting that whip sword in my Gundam's hand myself, I won't know for certain if this is the next great mech action game or not. The full game is out in March.

title: 《使命召唤：现代战争 4》战役抢先体验支持 DLSS 4.5，全新 GeForce Game Ready 驱动推出
text:
10 月 6 日，玩家可开始畅玩《战争机器：事变日》(Gears of War: E-Day) 和《星球大战：银河赛车手》(STAR WARS: Galactic Racer)，两款游戏现已推出并支持 DLSS 4.5。10 月还将迎来多款重磅新作与更新，包括 10 月 8 日推出的《养鬼吃人：复兴》(Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival)、10 月 9 日推出的《龙之信条 2：黑暗觉者》(Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen)，以及10 月 13 日推出的《微软飞行模拟 2024》(Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024) Sim Update 7。此外，《使命召唤：现代战争 4》(Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4) 战役抢先体验将于 10 月 16 日面向预购玩家开启，早于该游戏 10 月 23 日的正式发售。
NVIDIA 已发布全新 GeForce Game Ready 驱动，为《使命召唤：现代战争 4》(Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4)、《龙之信条 2：黑暗觉者》(Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen)、《微软飞行模拟 2024》(Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024) Sim Update 7、《星球大战：银河赛车手》(STAR WARS: Galactic Racer) 以及《不朽遗志》(Valor Mortis) 带来优化。玩家可通过 NVIDIA App 或 NVIDIA 官网下载该驱动。
以下为全新及即将推出的 RTX 游戏的详细介绍：
● 《使命召唤：现代战争 4》(Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4) ：朝鲜半岛战火燃起，在战役中，一支年轻的韩国士兵小队在崩溃的前线奋力求生，而在地球另一端，心怀复仇的普莱斯上尉在暗处展开个人之战，始终比追捕他的人抢先一步。战役抢先体验将于 10 月 16 日面向预购玩家开启，游戏将于 10 月 23 日正式发售，并支持全套 DLSS 4.5 技术。在所有模式中，DLSS 4.5 超分辨率可加速游戏运行并提升图像质量。在 GeForce RTX 40 系列PC上，DLSS 4.5 帧生成可进一步提升帧率。而在 GeForce RTX 50 系列PC上，玩家可开启动态多帧生成 6 倍模式，在图像质量与性能之间实现理想平衡，非常适合在启用可选光线追踪反射时充分提升帧率。此外，所有 GeForce RTX PC均可开启 NVIDIA Reflex，进一步降低 PC 延迟，让游戏操作响应更加灵敏。如需了解抢先体验的更多详情，查看页面了解更多详情。
● 《战争机器：事变日》(Gears of War: E-Day) ：现已推出。这部前传的故事发生在初代《战争机器》的 14 年前，讲述了马库斯·菲尼克斯和多姆·圣地亚哥的经历。玩家可在战役、Horde Siege PvE 和 Versus PvP 模式中体验 DLSS 4.5 超分辨率、帧生成、动态多帧生成、NVIDIA Reflex、RTX Mega Geometry 以及硬件加速光线追踪。在开启 6 倍多帧生成和 Ultra 光线追踪设置后，NVIDIA 表示，在 4K 分辨率下相比原生渲染平均性能提升 7.5 倍。
● 《007 初露锋芒》(007 First Light) ：免费 Extended Operations 更新新增两项战术模拟任务：以配备武器的阿斯顿·马丁 Valhalla 为特色的 Valhalla Protocol，以及背景设定在越南一家酒店的 Jungle Heist。此次更新还带来了 New Game+、全新武器与服装、装置切换、难度更高的“00”难度以及拍照模式。该游戏在 GeForce RTX PC 上支持路径追踪和 DLSS 4.5 光线重建。
● 《星球大战：银河赛车手》(STAR WARS: Galactic Racer) ：这是一款高风险竞速游戏的颠覆性新作，诞生于《星球大战》星系中无法无天的外缘星域。加入银河联赛——在风格各异的赛道上猛撞、撞击并击败对手，在这款以单局为单位的竞速冒险中，每一场比赛都截然不同。驾驶不同级别的反重力载具，包括陆行艇、飞行摩托、掠地飞车和标志性吊舱，每一种都拥有独特的物理特性和玩法风格。你可以独自踏上剧情驱动的战役，在变幻莫测的联盟中前行；也可投身策略性多人恩怨对决，在声誉相伴的较量中一较高下。 游戏已于10 月 5 日推出，首发即支持 DLSS 4.5 动态多帧生成和超分辨率，并支持硬件加速的光线追踪 Lumen 光照，DLSS 4.5 光线重建进一步提升其效果。请下载全新 GeForce Game Ready 驱动，其中包含多项优化。
● 《克里夫·巴克猛鬼追魂：复苏》(Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival) ：由 Saber Interactive 和 Boss Team Games 打造的《克里夫·巴克猛鬼追魂：复苏》(Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival)是一款全新单人求生恐怖动作游戏，背景设定在史上最具标志性的恐怖系列之一所构建的骇人宇宙中，演员道格·布拉德利近二十年来首次回归，再度出演其标志性角色针头人。玩家将跟随艾丹的故事，他必须解开神秘拼图盒“创世配置”的黑暗力量，从地狱般的深渊中救出女友。该游戏将于 10 月 8 日推出，支持 DLSS 超分辨率和帧生成。通过 NVIDIA App，玩家可升级至最新的 DLSS 模型，获得更出色的图像质量，并新增对动态帧生成的支持，最高可达 6 倍。
● 《真·三国无双 3：完全版 复刻版》(DYNASTY WARRIORS 3: Complete Edition Remastered) ：使《真·三国无双 3》(DYNASTY WARRIORS 3) 和《真·三国无双 3：猛将传》(DYNASTY WARRIORS 3: Xtreme Legends) 的精彩重现，这两部作品奠定了整个系列的基础。玩家可在三国世界中扮演 40 多位不同的武将，在广袤战场上体验一骑当千的激烈战术战斗，这些战场借助虚幻引擎 5 精美重现。该游戏现已推出，支持采用 NVIDIA 最新第二代 Transformer 模型的 DLSS 超分辨率，让 GeForce RTX 用户能够加速帧率并提升图像质量。
● 《微软飞行模拟 2024》(Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024) Sim Update 7 ：该免费更新将于 10 月 13 日推出，新增 National Championship Air Races，并对引擎进行更新和改进。它还将游戏升级至 DLSS 4.5，并引入多帧生成和动态多帧生成 6 倍模式。
● 《龙之信条 2：黑暗觉者》(Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen) ：该付费扩展包将于 10 月 9 日推出，在诺根地区带来全新剧情与遭遇，包括角色艾尔以及围绕不死堕落巨龙的谜团。玩家还可挑战 12 个地下城挑战以获取稀有装备，并用全新发型和纹身自定义角色。此次更新新增 DLSS 4.5，支持动态多帧生成和超分辨率，升级了游戏现有的 DLSS 帧生成和超分辨率集成。请务必下载全新 GeForce Game Ready 驱动，其中包含多项优化。
● 《控制：共振》(CONTROL Resonant) ：NVIDIA 全新游戏指南视频为玩家详解这款即将推出的游戏的图形设置和性能特性，包括 DLSS 4.5 和路径追踪。
